explanations.indigenous-depopulation-of-the-greater-a: The islands the sugar planters took in the seventeenth century had been emptied in the sixteenth. There was no indigenous labour force left in the Greater Antilles to compel, and the Lesser Antilles had never held one of the size a plantation economy needed; the labour was therefore bought and shipped. The cause here is a negative one and none the weaker for it — the decision to import Africans in those numbers was taken against the absence the previous century had made.

Spain took the Greater Antilles for gold and tribute, exhausted both, and left islands it barely occupied; the English, French and Dutch colonies of the seventeenth century were founded in and around that vacancy. Barbados itself is the extreme case: the cited account has the Amerindian settlement of the island ending in the early sixteenth century, so that the party of 1627 landed on ground with nobody on it. The type is the weak one: emptiness did not make sugar, it is what sugar was planted in.
explanations.italian-war-of-1494-1495--italian-wars-o: The Italian Wars of 1499–1504 article states the sequence as a condition and not as a cause: "In the aftermath of the Italian War of 1494–1498, Louis was determined to pursue French claims to Milan and Naples and in October 1499 he captured Milan, which remained in French hands for the next thirteen years." It adds what put Louis in a position to pursue them: "7 April 1498: Charles VIII of France died and was succeeded by his cousin Louis, Duke of Orléans as Louis XII. Louis had participated in the previous war, primarily in the 1495 Siege of Novara." The first war left the French claims unsettled and left the man who would press them next having fought in it; that is a precondition of the second and not its cause, which was a succession the first war did not bring about. Probable, because both articles are read at one revision each and neither names a historian for the reading. The 1499–1504 article calls the earlier war "Italian War of 1494–1498" where the record, taking its title from the item's own English article, calls it "Italian War of 1494–1495"; the two are the same war under two of English Wikipedia's own names and nothing here resolves which is right.
explanations.spanish-colonization-of-the-americas--sp: The expedition that became the conquest of Mexico set out from a colony that was already there, and the article says so in its own words: **"A well-connected settler in Cuba, Hernán Cortés received authorization in 1519 by the governor of Cuba to form an expedition of exploration-only to this far western region."** Twenty-six years of settlement in the Caribbean — the article gives the Spanish over two decades of exploring the islands and the mainland coast before this — are what put a governor in Havana with expeditions to license and a settler with the standing to lead one. The conquest is also filed as part of the colonization, which is a different statement: this link claims the licence and the base it came from, not that the colonization made the conquest inevitable.
explanations.spanish-colonization-of-the-americas--tr: The article puts the treaty after the settlement and as an answer to it: **"Once the Spanish settlement in the Caribbean occurred, Spain and Portugal formalized a division of the world between them in the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas."** It adds that Pope Alexander VI had divided rights to lands in the Western Hemisphere between the two crowns by the decree *Inter caetera* of 4 May 1493. The claim here is the sequence the article states and not a reading of who wanted the line drawn where.
explanations.the-first-columbian-voyage-1492--indigen: The demand for tribute in gold from every Taíno adult on Hispaniola began on the second voyage, in 1493, with hands cut off where it was not paid; the encomienda followed; the famine of 1495 and 1496 killed some fifty thousand; the population of the island was sixty thousand by 1507. Eighty to ninety per cent of the Taíno were dead within thirty years of the landfall. What is in dispute is which of the causes weighed most, and that is carried by its own edge; that the sequence begins with 12 October 1492 is not in dispute anywhere.
explanations.the-first-columbian-voyage-1492--spanish: This edge claims only what the article's first sentence states: the Spanish colonization of the Americas **"began in 1493 on the Caribbean island of Hispaniola after the initial 1492 voyage of Genoese mariner Christopher Columbus under license from Queen Isabella I of Castile"**. The voyage is what the settlement of 1493 followed from and was licensed under; the article says nothing about how much of what came after was decided by it, and neither does this link.
explanations.the-first-columbian-voyage-1492--the-atl: The same claim this milestone makes about Cabral’s landfall and for the same reason. Nothing about three ships in October 1492 predicts a traffic that began a century and a half later and was carried mostly by other powers. What the voyage did was make the islands a place Europeans went to, which every later step here needed and none of which it contains. The weak type, and it is the honest one: the chain is not an argument that Columbus caused the Atlantic slave trade.
explanations.the-first-columbian-voyage-1492--treaty-: The cited account of the treaty says what it was for in its first line of argument: it was intended to settle the dispute that arose following Columbus’s return in 1493, after he put in at Lisbon on his way back and John II claimed the new lands under an earlier bull. Twenty months from a landfall to a meridian is a short causal chain and the sources draw it themselves.
explanations.treaty-of-tordesillas-1494--portuguese-l: Cabral did not sail to find Brazil and the treaty did not send him; what the treaty did was decide in advance what a landfall there would mean. Taking possession in the name of Manuel I was an act with a legal addressee — Castile — and it worked because the coast lay east of the meridian agreed six years earlier. The claim here is narrow and is the weakest of the five types on purpose: the line did not cause the voyage, it is what made the voyage a claim.
explanations.treaty-of-tordesillas-1494--the-atlantic: The treaty is usually read for what it gave Portugal in the west. Read for what it left in the east it is the other half of the same fact: everything on the African side of the meridian stayed Portuguese, the Guinea and Angola coasts included. One crown therefore held both ends of a traffic that had not begun yet — the ports the captives were embarked at and the coast they were landed on. Wikipedia’s account of the Brazilian trade has most of the five and a half million embarking at West Central African ports, above all Luanda; that they were Portuguese ports is what 1494 settled.
explanations.voyages-of-christopher-columbus--spanish: The colonization article dates itself from the voyages and not from the first of them: "The Spanish colonization of the Americas began in 1493 on the Caribbean island of Hispaniola after the initial 1492 voyage of Genoese mariner Christopher Columbus" — 1493 is the second voyage, which carried settlers. The voyages article says the same from its end: the four expeditions "led to Europeans learning about the New World and were an early breakthrough in the period known in Europe as the Age of Exploration, which saw the colonization of the Americas". The atlas already carries the 1492 voyage as enabling the colonization; this edge is the other three voyages, which is what the colonization's own first sentence reaches back to. `enabled`, because a crossing that shows the way is not the decision to settle.
